sections.body_md:
A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and a full set of eigenvectors that can be chosen orthonormal. Those directions are the axes of the stretch. In that basis the matrix is diagonal, and each diagonal entry is the eigenvalue along one axis.

The factorization \(A = U D U^T\) says the same thing in the original coordinates. The factor \(U^T\) writes a vector in the eigenbasis, \(D\) multiplies each coordinate by its eigenvalue, and \(U\) returns to the original coordinates. Orthonormal columns are what make the inverse of \(U\) equal to \(U^T\). Finding the eigenvalues is the previous skill. This skill is the orthonormal basis and the product that rebuilds \(A\).

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md: For symmetric \(A\), \[ A = U D U^T, \qquad U^T U = I, \qquad D = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n). \] The inverse of \(U\) is \(U^T\). Rebuilding \(A\) is a sum of rank-one pieces \( \lambda_i u_i u_i^T \). On a positive semidefinite matrix the singular values agree with the absolute values of the eigenvalues.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 11 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\). The matrix is already diagonal, so the eigenbasis is the coordinate basis. The eigenvalues are 11 and 3. Their sum is the trace, 14, and their product is the determinant, 33.

Check the stretches. \(A(1,0) = 11(1,0)\) and \(A(0,1) = 3(0,1)\). The factorization is trivial: \(U\) is the identity and \(D\) holds 11 and 3. A vector such as \((1,1)\) is not an eigenvector, because \(A(1,1) = (11, 3)\) is not a scalar multiple of \((1,1)\). The two eigenvalues remain 11 and 3.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The identity \(A = U D U^{-1}\) is true for any diagonalizable matrix, but the transpose form needs orthonormal columns. A symmetric matrix can have nonzero off-diagonal entries and still be simple to diagonalize. The diagonal entries are not the eigenvalues unless the matrix is already diagonal. The zero vector satisfies \(A0 = \lambda 0\) for every \(\lambda\), so it is excluded from the definition of an eigenvector. Complex non-real eigenvalues do not occur for real symmetric matrices.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The Rayleigh quotient of a symmetric matrix sits between the smallest and largest eigenvalues and equals an eigenvalue at the matching eigenvector. Singular values of a general matrix are the square roots of the eigenvalues of \(A^T A\). Power iteration follows the eigenvalue of largest magnitude.
